lines: Ask a language model what the meaning of life is, and it will give you an answer.
Ask it which file on your computer is the largest, and it can't.
It can only write text.
An agent is what you get when you let that text do things.
In the next few minutes we will build one from nothing, piece by piece.
By the end, you will know how tools like Claude Code, Codex and OpenClaw work underneath.
It is simpler than you think.
Start with the brain.
A large language model does one thing: given some text, it predicts the next token, a word or a piece of a word.
Then it does it again, and again.
That is all.
It has no memory between calls, no clock, and no hands.
Everything it knows about your situation has to be in the text you send it.
That text is called the context.
So how does a chatbot remember the conversation?
It doesn't. The program does.
It keeps a list of messages: a system message with instructions, your message, and the model's reply.
Every time you say something, the whole list is sent again.
Here is a complete chatbot, in about ten lines of Python.
The list called context is the only memory there is.
Now the trick that turns a chatbot into an agent.
Along with the messages, we send a description of a tool: a name, what it does, and which arguments it takes. Here, a clock.
The model cannot run anything. But it can answer with a special message that says: please call the clock.
Our program sees that, runs the real function, and adds the result to the list as a new message.
Then we ask the model again. Now the time is in its context, and it can answer: tomorrow is Friday.
The model asks. The program acts.
Put that in a loop, and you have an agent.
Call the model. If it asks for tools, run them, add the results, and call it again.
If it answers without asking for a tool, it is done.
The model decides how many steps it needs. Our code only sets the maximum.
Every agent you have heard of, from coding assistants to personal assistants, is a variation of this loop.
Here is a real run, on a local model on a laptop.
The task: which Python file in this folder is the longest, and what does it do?
We never told it how. It lists the files.
Then it decides to count the lines with a shell command, and our program asks us for permission first.
It reads the longest file, and answers. Three tools, about thirteen seconds.
All we did was give it permission to look. It figured out the rest.

scenes.chapter: One tool to rule them all
lines: Tools can be anything a program can do: search the web, read a PDF, send an email, query a database.
One tool is special.
Give an agent a shell, and it can run any command on the computer.
Models have read millions of shell commands, so a single tool unlocks thousands of abilities.
That is how coding agents work. It is also why they can be dangerous.
Which brings us to the real engineering problem: the context.
Everything goes in it. The system prompt, the tool descriptions, the skills, the memory, the conversation, and every tool result.
And the whole thing is sent again on every single step.
It fills up fast. One long file can add thousands of tokens at once.
Bigger contexts cost more, and past a point, the model gets worse at using them.
So when the window is nearly full, agents compact. The model summarises the older part, and the summary replaces it. The latest messages are kept word for word.
Something is always lost. Deciding what to keep is the art.
This is why people now talk about context engineering, not prompt engineering.
The context disappears when the program stops. Memory is how an agent remembers across sessions.
The simplest version is a file. Give the agent a tool to write a note, and read the notes back into the context next time.
Real systems add search, either plain keyword search or vector search with embeddings, to pull in only the memories that matter.
And forgetting matters too. A memory full of trivia is just more noise in the context.
Skills solve the same problem for know-how.
A skill is a folder with a short description and a set of instructions.
At the start, only the one-line descriptions go into the context.
When a task matches, the agent loads the full instructions, and only then.
A hundred skills cost a hundred lines, not a hundred manuals. And an agent can even write new skills for itself.
Sub-agents are the same idea, one level up.
A sub-agent is just another context list, with its own instructions and tools, run through the same loop.
The main agent hands it a task. The sub-agent might read twenty files, but only its short report comes back.
The main context stays clean, and several sub-agents can work in parallel.
So far, the agent only acts when you type.
Autonomy means it can act on its own.
OpenClaw uses a heartbeat. Every thirty minutes the agent wakes up, reads a plain checklist file, does what is needed, and goes back to sleep.
You stay in control by editing the checklist.
More power means more risk. An agent that can send your email can send the wrong email.
Language models are not deterministic. And text from the outside world, a web page or a document, can contain instructions that try to take over the agent. This is called prompt injection.
So treat everything an agent reads as data, never as orders.
Give it the least access that gets the job done. Ask a human before anything that cannot be undone. Keep secrets out of reach. And log everything.
Capability and safety are a trade-off. Choose it deliberately.
That is the whole picture.
A model that predicts text. A list that holds the context. Tools that let the text act. And a loop that keeps going until the job is done.
Around it: compaction, memory, skills, sub-agents, and a heartbeat.
You can build every piece in an afternoon. The code for each step, the sources, and an interactive guide are linked below.
Build one yourself. It is the best way to understand where this is going.
